title: The subjunctive

objectives.can: Recognise present and aorist subjunctives by their long vowel and parse them.
Name the commonest uses of the subjunctive in a main clause and after ἐάν, ὅταν and ὃς ἄν.

explanation.summary: The subjunctive is the mood of what is not simply stated as fact: an exhortation, a question about what to do, a strong denial about the future, or a general supposition. It is recognised by its long thematic vowel, ω or η, and it has present and aorist forms that differ in aspect, not in time.

sections.heading: What a mood is
body: Mood is the speaker's way of putting a verb into the world. The indicative presents an action as a fact, or asks about a fact. The subjunctive does something different: the action is not announced but proposed, wondered about, denied for the future or supposed. A subjunctive is a finite verb, with person and number. It belongs to a tense stem (present, aorist or, rarely, perfect), and it never has an augment.

Do not translate the subjunctive with a fixed English word. English 'may', 'might' and 'should' fit some uses and badly mislead in others. In Hebrews 4:16 the subjunctive προσερχώμεθα is an invitation, 'let us approach'; in Matthew 6:2 the subjunctive ποιῇς after ὅταν is a general supposition, 'whenever you do'. The meaning comes from the construction the verb stands in, and this lesson teaches the commonest constructions.

sections.heading: How to recognise the forms
body: The subjunctive takes the stem of the tense and puts a long vowel in the place where the indicative has a short one. The thematic ο/ε of the indicative (λέγομεν, λέγετε) becomes ω/η (λέγωμεν, λέγητε). The endings in the active are -ω, -ῃς, -ῃ, -ωμεν, -ητε, -ωσι(ν); in the middle and passive they are -ωμαι, -ῃ, -ηται, -ώμεθα, -ησθε, -ωνται. The singular endings all have an iota subscript. The subjunctive of the present and of the aorist is built on the same endings: only the stem differs.

The first aorist active adds -σ- to the stem and then these endings, with no augment: for ἀκούω the aorist stem is ἀκουσ-, and the endings -σῃς, -σωμεν and -σητε follow. The second aorist uses the aorist stem itself, with the same endings; so ἔρχομαι gives the aorist subjunctive εἰσέλθῃ, 'he may go in', which differs from the present subjunctive only in its stem. The aorist passive puts -θ- before the endings and has a circumflex on them: γεννηθῇ, εὑρεθῇ. Contract verbs and verbs in -μι have the same vowels, only contracted or shifted: ποιῇς, ἀγαπῶμεν, παραδοῖ.

sections.heading: Present and aorist subjunctive: aspect, not time
body: A subjunctive does not mark past or present. Even the aorist subjunctive, which has no augment, is not a past tense. What the tense stem shows is the aspect, the way the action is seen. The present stem looks at it as going on, repeated or in progress. The aorist stem looks at it as a whole, a single event with a beginning and an end. In Matthew 6:2 the same verse has the two: ὅταν ποιῇς (present) is about giving whenever you give, as a practice; μὴ σαλπίσῃς (aorist) is about the act of sounding the trumpet as a single deed. The time of both lies in the future of the main verb or of the speaker's situation, and the context tells it.

In practice the aorist subjunctive is by far the commoner of the two in the New Testament. A writer uses the present stem when the extended or repeated character of the action matters, and the aorist when it does not. Neither choice is wrong.

sections.heading: The commonest uses
body: Hortatory subjunctive: the first person plural, in a main clause, urges a group to act. ἄγωμεν is 'let us go'. This is the way Greek says 'let us…'; the speaker includes himself. John 11:16 and Hebrews 4:16 are examples.

Deliberative subjunctive: a question that asks what to do or what is to be done, with the first person (rarely the third). Τί ποιήσωμεν; asks 'what are we to do?', not 'what will we do?'. The question may be real or rhetorical. Luke 3:10 and Matthew 6:31 have it.

Emphatic negation: οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive (more rarely the future indicative) is the strongest way to deny that something will happen. John 10:28 and John 8:51 are examples. The two negatives together are not a double negative in the English sense; they build up one strong denial about the future.

Indefinite clauses: after ἐάν, 'if', and after ὅταν, 'whenever', the subjunctive supposes a case that may or may not occur. After a relative pronoun the particle ἄν (or ἐάν) gives 'whoever, whichever': ὃς ἄν, ὃς ἐάν. The same pattern holds for ὅπου ἐάν, 'wherever'. These clauses state something general or something yet to happen. Matthew 5:19 uses ὃς ἐὰν and ὃς δ' ἂν in two clauses side by side.

misunderstandings: Reading the aorist subjunctive as past. It has no augment and no past meaning; its aorist stem only shows that the action is seen as a whole.

Translating every subjunctive with 'may' or 'might'. The mood has several jobs, and 'let us' for the hortatory, 'shall we' for the deliberative and 'whenever' or 'whoever' for the indefinite fit the Greek much better.

Confusing the subjunctive with the indicative. The difference in the first and second person plural is only a vowel: ἄγομεν (indicative) and ἄγωμεν (subjunctive). In the first person singular of the first aorist, the subjunctive and the future indicative are written alike (-σω); context and the particles around the verb decide.
Reading οὐ μή as 'not not' or as two separate negatives. Together they are one emphatic denial.

deeper.heading: Subjunctive and future
body: The forms of the subjunctive and the future indicative are often close, and the Greek of the New Testament sometimes uses one where classical Greek would use the other. After οὐ μή, after ἵνα and after some conjunctions, a copyist may write a future indicative or an aorist subjunctive, since ο and ω came to sound alike. This is a well-known source of textual variants. The edition you are reading may differ from another at such a place, and the choice does not usually change the meaning much.

deeper.heading: Why a long vowel
body: In early Greek the subjunctive was formed by lengthening the stem vowel. That is why the subjunctive endings are a long ω or η where the indicative has a short vowel. The system you see in the New Testament is the later and simpler one, in which the same endings are attached to every stem.
